text.content: If a downstream agent or external system reads this key after the failure, will it be able to tell that the failure occurred? A key holding its default value is ambiguous — it could mean the run hasn't started yet, or it could mean the writing agent failed. A key holding an unexpected value is detectable. A key holding a plausible but wrong value is the most dangerous — it looks correct but isn't.

It affects every agent that reads that key in the same session. Isolation requires either that the failing agent resets the key to a safe value before failing, or that downstream agents check the key's validity before using it.

text.content: Conflating recovery with retry.

rich_text.plain_text: Conflating recovery with retry.

text.content: Retrying a failed agent run is not the same as recovering state. If the Classifier fails and the system retries the Classifier, the retry may succeed and overwrite the stale values, but between the failure and the successful retry, the state was in a misleading condition. Recovery design addresses that window, not just the eventual successful outcome.

text.content: Summary

rich_text.plain_text: Summary

text.content: State recovery and failure isolation are the final layer of the memory and state architecture for any multi-agent system. Recovery defines what the system should look like after a failure, which keys hold what values, and whether the state is safely ready for the next input. Isolation defines which agents can corrupt shared state when they fail, and how to contain that corruption so it does not propagate.

Isolation defines which agents can corrupt shared state when they fail, and how to contain that corruption so it does not propagate.
